activity.title: a year ago today, I packed my bags and left australia. i’d been there for 5 years after getting stuck during covid lockdowns. in that time i directed two shorts, placed top 10 at sydney film festival, started a production company, and bootstrapped my first feature film, ‘i fall to pieces.’ then, i made the hardest decision of my life (so far!) to leave it all, come back to the US, return to college and pivot into growth. there were so many hard conversations before leaving. it really felt like blowing up a huge part of my life; giving up the relationships, the momentum, the name i’d spent five years building. a year in, though, people have asked me if i regret my decision. and the answer is no. i recognized that my professional growth was plateauing where i was, and that i had to go elsewhere. and while it definitely stung to start a data science degree from square one and get humbled by a bunch of 18-year-old freshmen in my cs classes, the people i’ve met and the things i’ve learned have more than made up for it. for anyone on the precipice of a big life pivot, know that the juice is probably worth the squeeze. (also ‘pieces’ is still on the way, i promise :)) ...more

if you want to understand taste, study film editing. after recently changing editors on my feature film, "I Fall to Pieces", i've been working on the latest version myself and am reminded of what qualities make a great editor: discernment. restraint. knowing when to throw out a pretty-looking shot because it doesn't advance the story or deepen our understanding of a character. do you see what i'm getting at? taste is not really thrown around as a buzzword in film (at least, not when i was working), but great editors practice those skills on a daily basis. i highly recommend reading "In the Blink of an Eye" by Walter Murch (editor on "The Godfather Trilogy", "Apocalypse Now", etc), one of the marquee books on editing and a stealth book about taste. what is a movie you've watched and gone "that had great editing"? ...more

a month before we were going into production on my feature film “I Fall to Pieces”, I fired my cinematographer. he had learned his craft working on blockbuster movies, where your camera department can often have hundreds of people, and millions of dollars at your disposal. this was not the case on my movie, which was an indie, baby-budget production. as a cinematographer under those conditions, you don’t have as many resources available to you. it requires a different approach to solving problems. and after it became clear to me that he was struggling to adapt, i made the (very difficult) phone call to end it there. a few weeks ago, i stepped into the role of marketing lead at V1, and it’s very tempting to apply a filmmaker’s perspective to content creation. but i’m now seeing that it’s getting in my way. as a filmmaker, my priority is to tell emotionally and intellectually engaging stories. they take longer to make which gives me more time to be thoughtful about every aspect. as a marketing lead, i need to build mindshare. and unlike with movies, i don’t get to assume that i have my audience’s attention. uploading content is fast and consuming it is even faster. it requires me to think less in the mode of “how do i best express this idea” and more like “how do i engineer this for the best possible engagement”, recognizing that great content is usually not a set of disparate posts but a series of outputs resulting from a consistent, interconnected system. i feel like i’m in my cinematographer’s shoes. for now. what is a bad habit you’ve tried to unlearn? ...more

The culture of Maxxing is endemic. Been working in sf for a few weeks now and this has been one of my biggest observations. Maxxing, as you all know, is a suffix meme that originated with the incel forum term “Looksmaxxing”, and while that specific group of people has grown, the frame has eclipsed the culture it came from and now everyone is treating aspects of their lives as things to be engineered for the best imagined output. “-maxxing” implies that there is a maximum you have yet to reach, and not doing so is a deficit of your own making. Anxiety is the new aspiration, and while most public use of this is meant to be funny, the irony is still a kind of armor for people doing the thing. The people making the jokes are still playing the game. This trend exists within the language of a generation of people who are increasingly holding a ruler up to their lives and experiences. Every problem is an optimization problem. Though i do think this “how do you do fellow kids” kind of marketing is quite funny. ...more

At a certain point, someone on your team has to be in charge. Not everyone can be the boss. In the weeks leading up to shooting "I Fall to Pieces", my newly-appointed cinematographer was keen on the idea of us shooting the film in ultra-widescreen (aspect ratio 2.39:1, what you might use for a Marvel movie). I preferred widescreen (1.85:1). Weeks before the shoot turned into days before the shoot, and while I had explained that the epic, panoramic ultra-wide was not a good fit for a domestic drama, he didn’t budge. So I told him a story about the making of one of my favorite movies. In 1966, on the set of Mike Nichols' “Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”, Nichols, the first-time film director, and producer-writer Ernest Lehman disagreed about whether or not Richard Burton's character should wear glasses. Nichols: for. Lehman: against. Lehman asked "Well, what happens if we get very close to shooting and we still disagree? And you think he should wear glasses and I don't?" And Nichols said, "Well, I'll kill you." I told this story to my cinematographer and he never mentioned ultra-wide again. ...more

part of being an adult is realizing how easy it is to accidentally fall down a hill (like this insane one i found on baker and broadway this morning!). but career-wise. in 2022, i deferred my studies at LMU to start a production company. had i not done that and graduated when i was supposed to in may 2023, i would’ve received my bachelor's in screenwriting 5 days into the hollywood writers' strike. i would have been out of a job before i ever got one. similarly, had i not made the jump to study data science when i did, i would have missed the window to learn about AI inside of one of the best universities in the world. a lot of our successes and our failures are not our fault. i think the only lesson is to follow the opportunities where you stand to learn the most, and recognize when it’s time to move on to the next one. but actually, this hill was so steep. ...more

Something has shifted in the air recently. These days, the AgentMail crew: - ships a lot - sleeps too little The customers have gotten a lot bigger. The team remains small. When I wasn't building, I always thought about what the opportunity cost of not doing it looked like. What was the next thing I could be doing? What did I actually want to do with my life? Now that you feel like you're doing what you want, you start to think about the opportunity cost of doing it. Especially when it gets hard. You see the work-life balance and the vacations and PTO.... man that seems pretty nice. But I started realizing the way out is always going to be there. No matter what you do. There's always another thing you wanna do. Man, that would be nice. But if you get a rare chance to do what feels like your life's work, why not be delusionally optimistic? Why not love the late nights and the hard weeks and everything else that comes with it? Why not give everything and all to it? There's always going to be a shiny new thing to chase. But I heard once that you don't realize the good days until you've left them. And man, do I feel good about what we're building :)

For AgentMail to win, it needs to be one of the most distributed products of all time. Every AI agent is going to need an email address, an identity, and a way to talk to the rest of the world. We want to be the thing they all use. That means being in every framework, every doc, every Discord, and every model's answer when someone asks what to build on. We just opened up THREE new roles and are assembling the Avengers of AgentGrowth now: Founding GTM and Operations Lead. You own how we grow. Outbound, content, partnerships, launches, plus the dashboards and processes that hold it together. Founding PLG and Community Lead. Reddit, Discord, X, hackathons, dinners, and our office in SF. Almost everything that has worked for us came from builders finding us in a thread and telling their friends. You'd own that, plus the expanded budget and all the experiments we run on our funnel. Agent Experience Engineer. Our biggest user is not a person. It's an agent that reads our docs, asks a model what to use, and signs up on its own. This role owns all of it. AEO, evals, benchmarks, agent traces, and the docs themselves. Very few people have this job anywhere right now - but everyone will in a few years. The bar is high, so $15k your way if you can point us to someone we like :)

What’s one thing you’ve built with AI that saves you time from work you used to hate doing?

You should take more chances in your marketing. One thing I love about our company is that we've never been scared to pull a stunt. Some of the highlights: putting up a tweet on a billboard in the middle of North Beach. Buying a physical mailbox and telling our lead investor we pivoted. Trusting an AI agent with tens of thousands of dollars and letting it give company money away. It's paid off. Big. Every.Single.Time. Here's the part I don't talk about. Before every single one of these, I often get anxious and this sinking feeling of dread. What will people think? What happens if this goes wrong? What if it flops and I end up looking stupid? When you're early on in building, that feeling is hard to get past. What helped me was flipping the question around. Instead of what happens if this goes wrong... what happens if it works? What if it goes exactly the way you drew it up? Something I've picked up along the way is that you are usually your own biggest blocker. You put constraints on yourself that nobody gave. You invent an audience in your head and then spend all your energy trying not to embarrass yourself in front of people who were never watching. And that's the thing. Nobody cares if a launch flops, because nobody saw it. So relaunch. Now and in the future, it costs nothing to build and ship a product now. Everyone has the same tools. The scarce thing isn't the product anymore, it's attention. And attention usually never goes to the safest thing in the room. So take the chance. Don't be scared to look stupid. People pay attention to people at the end of the day, and I don't think that's changing anytime soon :)
